newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Nordics offer homes to "train of despair" refugees.
newsitem.headline: Nordics offer homes to "train of despair" refugees.

text.p: Sweden, Denmark, Finland and Norway have agreed to give homes to a group of 108 Middle Eastern refugees, allowing them to end a nightmarish journey to the West which has lasted almost two years.

The group spent 16 days on trains being shuttled between between Latvia, Lithuania and Russia in what was called a "train of despair" before being allowed to settle at the Olaine open prison outside Riga in April 1995.

"There's been a meeting in Helsinki with Nordic ministers for immigration. They decided to give resident permits to 108 people from the Olaine camp," said Pekka Johansson, a political advisor to Swedish Foreign Aid Minister Pierre Schori on Wednesday.
Sweden will give 52 of the refugees visas to settle in the country permanently, Johansson told Reuters. Denmark will accept 25, Finland, 20, and Norway the other 11.
Sweden's immigration authority said it hoped the refugees assigned to them could come to Sweden before Christmas.
"We will do everything in our power to make this happen," Ruben Ahlvin, a spokesman for Sweden's Invandrarverket, told national Swedish news agency TT.
Most of the group are from Iraq and nearly half are children. Some have relatives living in the Nordic countries.
"They will be placed in the communities where their relatives live," TT quoted Ahlvin as saying.
The group travelled from their homes via Moscow, where police say the Russian mafia organise hazardous and expensive journeys for people desperate to leave their homelands.
From Moscow, the travellers went to Latvia, where their boat to Sweden went aground on an Estonian island and they were eventually returned to Riga.
The group said they hid in Riga until they were caught on March 21 last year, when they began their train journey as Latvia tried to expel them.

The train sparked a diplomatic row between Moscow and Riga, which said it had neither the legal framework to send immigrants back to where they came nor the financial or physical resources to look after them.

The United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) slammed Latvia for holding the migrants in the train carriages, which were unsanitary and unheated, and said the refugees were being treated like cattle.
Their next home, the Olaine open prison 25 km (15 miles), was only slightly better. Escapees from the camp said the heating system was faulty and medicine and food were sparse.
Some of the group said they had paid $2,500 for their transport to Sweden.
